name: Shannon Estuary
summary: Where the river meets the sea between the Silvermine and Lough Gur: Connla on its pontoons, Ceannoi on the road south, the eriu siabra, the ollipheist and the four stones.

facts.text: In Irish myth the river Shannon is named for Sinann, who went to Connla's Well seeking wisdom; the well burst its banks and drowned her, and its water carried her to the sea.
Ollphéist ('great beast') is the name of the water-serpents and dragons of Irish folklore; arracht means a monster or apparition.

story:
The river that comes down past Lough Gur and the Silvermine meets the sea at the Shannon Estuary, and the harpers of Connla sing every visitor the same song about it before they will sing anything else. Sinann went looking for wisdom at Connla's Well, the song goes, where the hazels let fall their nuts into the water and the salmon eat them, and she was greedy, or brave, or only thirsty, and the well rose up out of its banks and drowned her and carried her down to the sea, and the water she rode is the river. The estuary is where she reached the sea. The fishers of Connla say the water still tastes faintly of hazelnut at the turn of the tide, and they do not mean it as a joke.

Connla took the well's name and stands on the estuary's western shore, half on land and half on pontoons over the water, a town of fishers and boatmen and teachers of every path, where the young of the realm learn to swim before they learn anything else, because the pontoons move. Kyli keeps the pontoon end. Criofan the fisherman keeps the bridge north of town and complains about the siabra who steal his catch. The road from Connla runs east past a guard post toward Innis Carthaig and Lough Gur, and south over the hills to Ceannoi, a merchants' stop on the high road, where the armourers sell scale to anyone going further.

The siabra of the estuary call themselves eriu, after the oldest name of the land itself, the name the first people gave it before any of the rest of us came, and they say it is theirs by right. The eriu henters keep the eastern hills above the river and the eriu fiscere fish the shore south of the stepping-stone bridge, and between them they hold the estuary's east bank as the Cullen siabra hold the bog. Kaen Kedger keeps a house on the hillside of their camp, and Solas walks the road with them, and further up, by four stone slabs north-east of Ceannoi, waits Abbadona, a demon the realm found where a master mentalist's vision said the Dagda's harp would lead.

At the river's mouth the ollipheist breed. They are the great water-serpents of the old stories, younger and smaller here than the ones in the songs but still longer than a boat, and they come up the shore at the river mouth in the south-west where the water is brackish. Arracht, which the fishers say is only the word for a monster, haunts the hill above them. The far liath rolls in off the sea on the same shore and leads people into the water, and the fishers tie a rope to their belts when they go out in fog.

North of Connla there is a grove of dead trees, and in it Ciar, a woman of the willow who died and would not lie down, and across the estuary her guardian Lucan, who cannot rest while she walks; the young of Tir na Nog are sent to cut the willow and let him go. South of Connla four standing stones stand in a field, and at night Osier comes to them, and the women of Ardee send for a bladder of a wolfhound and water from a dew sheerie to free him. On the curves of the road to Ceannoi a thief called Nasco used to walk at night with a spear that was not his, and Aziliz of the lake wants it back for Howth.

Why does it matter? Because the estuary is where the realm's water ends. Everything the rivers carry out of the hills passes Connla on its way to the sea: silver dust from the Silvermine, peat from the bog, the lake's music on summer nights. The harpers say the river is still Sinann, still carrying away what she drank, and that a wise person drinks from it only once, at the turn of the tide, and only a little.
legend: Shannon Estuary, between the Silvermine and Lough Gur, levels 1-38. Connla (west shore) is the town: trainers of every path, channeler, and lots of quests (Harper Cadwr has eleven, including The Touch of Amadan Duhb). Ceannoi on the road south is a merchant stop. Low camps round Connla (mudmen, spraggons, rowdies, beach rats, crabs), then giant ants (28-37), moss sheeries, the eriu siabra on the east bank (henters 31-36, fiscere 26-27, social), walking rocks and spraggonix in the north-east, ollipheist (34-38) at the river mouth in the south-west. Named: Abbadona (45, 'the demon Abbadona' of The Lost Relics, met after you play the Dagda's Harp at the four stone slabs) high in the east, Arracht (38), Danderpaw (36), Kaen Kedger (Criofan's Fish), Nasco (night, Search for Nasco's Spear). The pontoons move: mind your footing. Fishers' custom: tie a rope to your belt in fog, and drink from the river only once.

loremaster.intro: The Shannon Estuary, where [Sinann] reached the sea. [Connla] took the well's name; [Ceannoi] keeps the high road. The [eriu] hold the east bank; the [ollipheist] breed at the river mouth; and north of Connla [Ciar] walks.

topics.Sinann: In the harpers' song, the woman who went to Connla's Well for wisdom and was drowned by it and carried to the sea. The river is her road. The fishers say the water tastes of hazelnut at the turn of the tide.
topics.Connla: The town on the estuary's western shore, half on pontoons. Fishers, boatmen and teachers of every path. Kyli keeps the pontoon end, Harper Cadwr the songs, Criofan the bridge to the north.
topics.Ceannoi: A merchants' stop on the high road south of [Connla], where armourers sell scale to anyone going further. Nasco used to walk the road's curves at night.
topics.eriu: The siabra of the estuary, who take their name from the land's oldest name and say it is theirs. Henters on the eastern hills, fiscere on the shore; Kaen Kedger and Solas among them.
topics.ollipheist: The great water-serpents of the old stories, younger and smaller here than in the songs, breeding at the river mouth in the south-west. Arracht haunts the hill above them.
topics.Ciar: A woman of the willow who died in the grove of dead trees north of [Connla] and would not lie down. Her guardian Lucan, across the estuary, cannot rest while she walks.
topics.four stones: Four standing stones in a field south of [Connla]. Osier comes to them at night. The women of Ardee know how to free him: a wolfhound's bladder and a dew sheerie's water.
topics.Abbadona: A demon waiting by four stone slabs on the high ground north-east of [Ceannoi]. The master mentalist's vision sent the seekers of the Dagda's harp there; the harp was played, and Abbadona answered. Lobais was misled, and says so.
topics.Cadwr: Harper Cadwr of [Connla], who sings [Sinann]'s song to every visitor before anything else, and sends the young to cure the Amadan's touch.
topics.Kaen Kedger: The kedgers of the eriu are the siabra who catch fish, and Kaen is the best of them, with a house of his own behind the kedger camp on the eastern hillside. Criofan the fisherman of Connla had a golden fish for a pet, and the fish swallowed his pearl ring and swam up the river, and Criofan is sure Kaen caught it. He is right. Kaen keeps the fish in a bowl in his house, the eriu say, and has not yet thought to look inside it.
topics.Nasco: On the curves of the road to [Ceannoi] walks a thief called Nasco, with a spear that is not his. Aziliz of Lough Derg, the prophetess, wants the spear back for Howth, and says it was taken from a Howth grave, and that Nasco took to the road with it by night because nobody walks that road by night who has any sense. The Ceannoi merchants say he walks it by day too, now. Old thieves grow bold.
topics.Solas: Solas is one of the eriu siabra who walks the road near [Ceannoi], and he is the one Aziliz sends the young to when she wants to know what the gurite siabra are doing at Lough Gur. He knows, and he will tell, for a price: the head of a curmudgeon fighter, which he wants for reasons of his own. Solas means light, the harpers of Connla say. He has never explained the name, and he does not seem to like the sun.
topics.Lethe: Lethe is a rowdy of the estuary flats, one of the big quarrelsome men who drink and fight along the river, and the only one with a name, which he gave himself. It is a scholar's name, from a river in a southern tale whose water makes the drinker forget. Lethe drinks from the Shannon and forgets nothing, the Connla harpers say, which is his trouble. He wanders among the mudmen and the frogs of the flats and picks fights with them.
topics.Muir: Muir is the sea, in the old tongue, and Muir is what the river folk north of [Connla] call the koalinth who swims up the estuary from the open water every season and lies in their shallows as if he owned them. He is larger than the koalinth of the caverns. Chief Gaeth of the river folk, who keeps a camp close by and does not fight him, says the sea sends him to see how far the river has come, and that one day the sea will want it back.
topics.Kirwyn: Kirwyn is an eriu who stands near Lucan, the guardian of Ciar's dead willow grove, and does not let him rest. Lucan asked the young of the realm to free him from Ciar's charge, and they did, and he still stands where he stood, and Kirwyn still stands beside him, a siabra watching a ghost. The Connla folk think Kirwyn was the one who killed Lucan, long ago, and has never been able to leave the place either.
topics.Srandamar: Far east of [Connla], where the estuary's hills give out, two stone imps stand on a rise, carved by nobody anyone remembers, and the lesser zephyrs blow round them. Above them flies Srandamar, a deamhan of the air, pale as the zephyrs, and the herders say the statues were carved to keep him there, and that they work, for he has never flown further. They also say nobody should move the statues. Nobody has.

book.title: The River's Last Mile, by Harper Cadwr of Connla
pages: Every harper of Connla sings Sinann first. It is the town's law, older than the pontoons. She went to the well for wisdom, and the well rose and took her and carried her to the sea, and the river is the road she took. I sing it to the young who come through on their way to Lough Gur and they look at me as if I were selling them something. I am. I am selling them the idea that water can be dangerous because it is wise, which is the only idea that keeps anyone alive in this town.

Connla is built half on the water, on pontoons that move with the tide, and the first thing we teach the young is to swim, because the second thing they will do is fall in. Kyli keeps the far end and watches the boats. Criofan fishes from the bridge to the north and blames the siabra. The siabra of the east bank call themselves eriu, the land's first name, and say the river was theirs before it was Sinann's. They may be right. They are not polite about it, and they fish our shore at night as if to prove it.

At the river mouth the great serpents breed. They are the ollipheist of the old stories, or their grandchildren, and they come up the brackish shore in the south-west in the spring and lie in the shallows like fallen trees. Something the fishers will only call the monster haunts the hill above them. The grey fog comes in off the sea on that shore. When it does, the fishers tie ropes to their belts and to the posts, and the ropes are still there in the morning, mostly. We count the knots.

North of town there is a grove of dead willow, and a woman in it who should have lain down long ago, and across the water her guardian waiting for her to stop. South of town there are four stones, and someone who comes to them at night. Everything the rivers carry out of the hills passes us on its way to the sea, and some of it stops. The harpers say drink from the river only once, at the turn of the tide, and only a little. I have done it once.
